query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn system was selected to reduce cost while retaining the mechanical performance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi; prior work reported comparable or better mechanical properties after excluding Co. Research on FeNiCrMn has mainly addressed corrosion, while studies of related high- and medium-entropy alloys examined dynamic responses under tension or compression, different temperatures and strain rates, compositional changes, and the presence of cracks or voids. Those studies established that dynamic properties are sensitive to loading regime and material condition, but their different chemistries and defect states do not identify what governs FeNiCrMn. Under the constraints of retaining the Co-free composition and its strength–ductility balance, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains the dynamic behavior of solidified FeNiCrMn across temperature and strain-rate regimes? Define a controlled study capable of testing the hypothesis, its applicable boundaries, the prior findings that support it, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The dynamic mechanical behavior of solidified Co‐free FeNiCrMn is governed by the interplay between dislocation slip and a rapid, strain rate– and temperature–dependent dislocation healing (or re-strengthening) mechanism. This balance produces avalanche‐like plastic events (serrations) that underlie its strength–ductility performance across different loading regimes.
generation.material_initial_state: Co–free FeNiCrMn alloy that has been solidified and thermally treated to produce a uniform, low‐defect microstructure similar to that of the benchmark CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
generation.intervention: Dynamic mechanical testing under controlled tension or compression at varied strain rates and temperatures, combined with in situ microstructural characterization (e.g., high-speed digital image correlation and synchrotron X-ray diffraction) and concurrent mesoscale dislocation dynamics simulations.
generation.conditions: Temperature range from ambient to approximately 1073 K; strain rates spanning from 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹ (quasi-static) up to high strain-rate conditions (e.g., 10³ s⁻¹); an inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation; and tests performed under both tension and compression to ensure symmetry of response.
generation.structural_mediator: The evolution of dislocation structures, including the formation of slip bands and localized weak spots that are rapidly healed or re-strengthened between avalanche events.
generation.mechanism: At lower strain rates or elevated temperatures, dislocations have enough time to rapidly reorganize and heal, resulting in relatively smooth plastic flow. Conversely, at high strain rates and/or lower temperatures, the healing process lags behind dislocation slip, leading to sudden stress drops (avalanche-like events) and increased strain rate sensitivity. This dynamic balance governs the alloy’s mechanical response across temperature and strain rate regimes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stress–strain curves will show pronounced serrated flow (indicative of slip avalanches) under high strain-rate/low-temperature conditions and smoother curves under low strain-rate/high-temperature conditions. In situ microstructural observations will correlate these macroscopic stress fluctuations with variations in dislocation density and localized slip band formation, as predicted by the simulations.
generation.baseline: The established strength–ductility balance and moderate strain rate sensitivity observed at room temperature and intermediate strain rates in the analogous CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to solidified Co–free FeNiCrMn alloys with a uniform, low-defect microstructure, and under dynamic loading where dislocation slip (as opposed to other mechanisms like twinning or grain boundary sliding) is expected to be the dominant deformation mode.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative contributions of dislocation healing versus slip kinetics remain to be determined. Additionally, while the hypothesis focuses on dislocation mechanisms, potential contributions from other processes (such as incipient twinning or shear band localization under extreme conditions) cannot be entirely ruled out without further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a controlled series of dynamic mechanical tests on solidified Co–free FeNiCrMn samples across a broad range of strain rates and temperatures. Integrate high-speed digital image correlation and in situ synchrotron X-ray diffraction to monitor the evolution of dislocation structures during deformation. Concurrent meso-scale dislocation dynamics simulations will provide a comparative framework to identify the predicted avalanche-like events and healing behaviors.
measurements: Stress–strain curves to identify the magnitude and frequency of serrations under different testing conditions
Real-time microstructural imaging capturing dislocation density, slip bands, and possible shear localization
Temperature-dependent measurements of dislocation healing rates and rearrangement dynamics
Comparative analysis between experimental observations and simulation results.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If dynamic tests fail to reveal a consistent correlation between strain rate/temperature and the occurrence of avalanche-like stress drops attributable to dislocation slip with concomitant rapid healing, or if an alternative mechanism (such as predominant twinning or grain boundary sliding) is found to govern the dynamic behavior across the tested regimes, then this hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are new alloys that contain five or more elements in roughly-equal proportion. We present new experiments and theory on the deformation behavior of HEAs under slow stretching (straining), and observe differences, compared to conventional alloys with fewer elements. For a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates, HEAs deform in a jerky way, with sudden slips that make it difficult to precisely control the deformation. An analytic model explains these slips as avalanches of slipping weak spots and predicts the observed slip statistics, stress-strain curves, and their dependence on temperature, strain-rate, and material composition. The ratio of the weak spots’ healing rate to the strain-rate is the main tuning parameter, reminiscent of the Portevin-LeChatellier effect and time-temperature superposition in polymers. Our model predictions agree with the experimental results. The proposed widely-applicable deformation mechanism is useful for deformation control and alloy design.

The effect of changing temperatures and adding elements to alloys ranging from FCC-LEAs to FCC-HEAs has been studied to investigate the PLC effect at a strain-rate of 10−4/s. The effect of varying the strain-rates from 1 × 10−5 to 1 × 10−2/s on the serration behavior was examined. The PLC effect is observed in a specific range of temperatures and strain-rates for MEAs and HEAs, and not in LEAs representing the conventional substitutional alloys. As shown in the above six observations, the experimental results agree with the model introduced above. Although the pinning mechanism of such alloys is different from that in conventional alloys with low solute contents, their serrations can be explained as avalanches of slipping weak spots. The main difference is that in MEAs and HEAs, the weak spots (or dislocations) weaken upon slipping and re-strengthen (or in-situ pin) at a relatively fast healing rate between avalanches, compared to conventional alloys. In addition, the PLC effect is more pronounced in HEAs than in MEAs. frame.goal: To elucidate a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis that explains the dynamic mechanical behavior (response under tension/compression across a range of temperatures and strain rates) of the FeNiCrMn alloy.
frame.limitation: Prior studies on related high- and medium-entropy alloys have not isolated a singular mechanism that governs the dynamic response of Co-free FeNiCrMn, especially given the influence of loading regime and material condition.

frame.regime: Dynamic testing under controlled tension or compression at various strain rates and temperatures, with a focus on capturing the alloy’s behavior under both low and high strain-rate regimes.
